sense: the way in, an entrance (the place)

evidence: Caes. B.G. 5.9: omnēs introitūs erant praeclūsī (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Caecin. 8: ad omnēs introitūs, quā adīrī poterat (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The place where one goes in, of a building, a harbour (Caes. B.C. 3.39) or a wood; also the going in itself (see entry, the going in).
The way one approaches a place, and so its entrance; also the chance of approaching a person (see access).

phrases.latin: angustō in aditū taurus luctāns cornibus cum vix intrāre posset ad praesēpia, mōnstrābat vitulus quō sē pactō plecteret
phrases.english: when a bull, struggling with his horns in a narrow entrance, could hardly get in to his stall, a calf showed him how to twist himself

sources: Lewis & Short: introitus · Lewis & Short: aditus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 310.
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-phaedrus), checked against the editions named there. Caesar and Cicero as Lewis & Short quotes them.
